name: Unification of Italy
info: The Unification of Italy, or Risorgimento, was the 19th-century political and social movement that joined the states of the Italian Peninsula into the Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed in 1861 and completed with the capture of Rome in 1870.

facts.where: the Italian Peninsula and its outlying isles: Piedmont and Sardinia, Lombardy and Venetia, the central duchies, the Papal States, the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and Sicily; exiles worked from France and elsewhere abroad
facts.period: revolts of the 1820s and 1830s; revolutions and the First War of Independence 1848–1849; Second War of Independence 1859; Garibaldi's expedition 1860; Kingdom of Italy proclaimed 1861; Third War of Independence 1866; capture of Rome 1870; capital moved to Rome 1871
facts.figures: Giuseppe Mazzini, founder of Young Italy; Giuseppe Garibaldi, leader of the Expedition of the Thousand; Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, Prime Minister of Piedmont; Victor Emmanuel II, King of Sardinia and then of Italy; Charles Albert, King of Sardinia until 1849
facts.outcome: the Kingdom of Italy under the House of Savoy, with Rome as capital from 1871; Italian speakers in Trentino and Venezia Giulia remained outside its borders until 1918–1920

t: The Congress of Vienna of 1814–15 restored the old patchwork of Italian governments, and risings against it in the 1820s and 1830s were put down with Austrian help.
After the failed revolutions of 1848–1849 the patriots concluded that unification would need a strong monarchy under Piedmont, the expulsion of Austria with French help, and not the pope as leader.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861 and Rome was captured on 20 September 1870, but the new state was built on Piedmont's institutions and left lasting regional grievances.
dyk: From 1859 the slogan "Viva VERDI" spread through Italy as an acronym for Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia, a cry for King Victor Emmanuel II.
ev: A regiment of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies under the Carbonaro Guglielmo Pepe mutinies and wins a constitution that Austrian troops soon overturn
The Milanese expel the Austrian garrison in the Five Days of Milan, and Charles Albert of Sardinia declares war on Austria
A Roman Republic is proclaimed on 9 February and falls to a French force on 29 June, as Venice surrenders to Austria in August
Garibaldi sails from Quarto with about a thousand volunteers and takes Sicily and Naples
The first Italian Parliament proclaims Victor Emmanuel King of Italy on 17 March
Italy allies with Prussia against Austria and receives Venetia
The Italian army breaches the Aurelian Walls at Porta Pia and enters Rome

sections.background:
Italy was unified by the Roman Republic in the latter part of the third century BCE and, after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, lost its unity for centuries. It gradually developed into a system of city-states, with the Kingdom of Sicily or Naples in the south and the Papal States in the centre. Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Machiavelli and Guicciardini expressed a desire to see Italy become a unified nation, and in 1764 Gian Rinaldo Carli's Della Patria degli Italiani reflected a sense of Italian national identity.

The French Revolutionary Wars of 1792–97 set up a series of client republics. French rule destroyed the old structures of feudalism in Italy and introduced modern ideas and efficient legal authority, and it provided much of the intellectual force and social capital that fuelled unification movements for decades. After Napoleon fell, the Congress of Vienna of 1814–15 restored the pre-Napoleonic patchwork of governments, and Austria controlled Lombardy–Venetia directly and the duchies of Parma, Modena and Tuscany indirectly.

Denis Mack Smith argues that few people in 1830 believed an Italian nation might even exist: there were eight states with distinct laws, and the common people spoke mutually unintelligible dialects, wanted good government rather than self-government and had welcomed the French as more efficient than their native dynasties.
sections.aims:
The movement's supporters held three ideals of unification. In 1842 the Piedmontese priest Vincenzo Gioberti suggested a confederation of Italian states under the leadership of the pope. Giuseppe Mazzini and Carlo Cattaneo wanted a federal republic, which proved too extreme for most nationalists. Cesare Balbo proposed the middle position, a confederation of separate Italian states led by Piedmont. Mazzini, while in prison, formulated a programme for a free, independent and republican nation with Rome as its capital, and his society Young Italy took the mottos "God and People" and "Union, Strength and Freedom".

The Carbonari, a secret society that spread across Italy, sought to defeat tyranny and establish constitutional government. They took their principles of liberty, equality and fraternity from the French Revolution and were strongly anticlerical. Italian exiles abroad, immersed in European ideas, called for a masculine response to what Europeans saw as Italian vices, and they fashioned their image of the future nation on the standards of European nationalism.

After the defeats of 1848–1849 the patriots drew three lessons. They had to expel Austria first, even at the price of whatever France asked in return. The pope was an enemy and could never lead a united Italy. Republicanism was too weak a force, so unification had to rest on a strong monarchy, in practice Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II. The movement's later motto was "Free from the Alps to the Adriatic".
sections.events:
In 1820 a regiment of the army of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, commanded by the Carbonaro Guglielmo Pepe, mutinied and King Ferdinand I agreed to a constitution. The revolutionaries failed to court popular support and fell to Austrian troops of the Holy Alliance, after which Ferdinand abolished the constitution and persecuted known revolutionaries. In 1821 troops at Alessandria adopted the green, white and red tricolore in the Piedmont revolt led by Santorre di Santarosa, but King Charles Felix disavowed the constitution on his return and Di Santarosa's troops were defeated. In 1831 the Duke of Modena arrested Ciro Menotti with Austrian help and Menotti was executed. The Austrian army then slowly crushed the risings in the Papal Legations and Parma.

In 1844 Attilio and Emilio Bandiera, members of Young Italy, landed near Crotone with about twenty men, were betrayed and, with nine companions, were executed by firing squad. In 1848 revolts began in Sicily and Naples, and on 18 March the Milanese and Venetians rose; the Austrian garrison was expelled from Milan after five days of street fighting. Charles Albert of Sardinia declared war on Austria but was defeated at Custoza on 24 July and at Novara on 23 March 1849. A Roman Republic proclaimed on 9 February 1849 fell to a French force on 29 June, and Venice surrendered to the Austrians on 24 August.
sections.people:
Giuseppe Mazzini organised Young Italy at Marseille after his release from prison in 1831 and became Chief Minister of the Roman Republic in March 1849. Giuseppe Garibaldi, a native of Nice, was sentenced to death after a Piedmont uprising in 1834, escaped to South America and spent fourteen years in exile, where he learned the art of guerrilla warfare. On 6 May 1860 he sailed from Quarto near Genoa with about a thousand volunteers, landed near Marsala, won at Calatafimi on 13 May and declared himself dictator of Sicily in the name of Victor Emmanuel. He entered Naples on 7 September and later handed over his dictatorial power to the king at Teano.

Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour (1810–1861), a modernizer interested in agrarian improvements, banks, railways and free trade, became prime minister of Piedmont in 1852. He brought the kingdom into the Crimean War as an ally of Britain and France in 1855 and found an ally in Napoleon III in 1859. He died in June 1861; when given the last rites he purportedly said: "Italy is made. All is safe."

Victor Emmanuel II succeeded his father Charles Albert in 1849 and was given the epithet Father of the Fatherland. Pope Pius IX had at first appeared a reformer and granted a constitution to the Papal States on 21 February 1848, but he turned against liberalism and nationalism and fled Rome in November 1848.
sections.outcomes:
In April 1859 Cavour found an ally in Napoleon III and the Second War of Italian Independence began. The Austrians lost at Magenta and Solferino, and by the Armistice of Villafranca on 12 July Lombardy went to Sardinia while Austria kept the Veneto and Mantua. Sardinia annexed central Italy on 22 March 1860 and gave Savoy and Nice to France on 24 March. After Garibaldi's campaign in the south, the first Italian Parliament proclaimed Victor Emmanuel King of Italy on 17 March 1861. Italy received Venetia in 1866 after a referendum in which 69 of more than 642,000 ballots opposed annexation; historians suggest it was held under military pressure. On 20 September 1870 the Bersaglieri entered Rome through a breach at Porta Pia, where 49 Italian soldiers and four officers and nineteen papal troops died. Rome and Latium were annexed after a plebiscite on 2 October.

Historians have stressed the cost. Martin Clark says, "It was Piedmontization all around": the constitution, tax rates, officials and top military posts were Piedmont's, and Cavour's promises of regional and local government were broken in 1861. The first decade saw savage insurrections in Sicily and the Naples region. The pope ordered the Catholic Church not to co-operate with the new government, a decision fully reversed only in 1929.
sections.legacy:
Italian unification is still debated. Massimo d'Azeglio said: "Italy has been made. Now it remains to make Italians." Francesco Saverio Nitti criticised the new state for ignoring the economic differences between north and south, which he held to be the cause of the southern question. Gaetano Salvemini held that a lack of understanding and action by politicians let corruption and organised crime flourish in the south, and Antonio Gramsci criticised the limited presence of the masses in politics and the lack of land reform. Denis Mack Smith, Christopher Duggan and Lucy Riall are among the authors who continue to review its successes and failures.

Many Italian speakers in Trentino and Venezia Giulia remained outside the kingdom, which gave rise to Italian irredentism. The annexation of Trento and Trieste in 1918 is often considered the culmination of the movement, and some historians see the Risorgimento as continuing to the Treaty of Rapallo in 1920. Historians regard the "mutilated victory" rhetoric that Mussolini adopted as a political myth.

Italy celebrates the anniversary of the unification on 17 March. Il Canto degli Italiani, first performed publicly in 1847, has been the national anthem since 1946. Historians disagree on how political Verdi's operas were: Franco Della Peruta stresses his patriotic intent, while Roger Parker argues that nationalistic historians exaggerated it.

summary: The Unification of Italy, or Risorgimento, joined the states of the Italian Peninsula into the Kingdom of Italy between the failed revolts of the 1820s and the capture of Rome in 1870. It rested on Piedmont's monarchy, French and Prussian wars against Austria, and Garibaldi's volunteers.
references: Derek Beales, The Risorgimento and the Unification of Italy (Longman, 2003)
Harry Hearder, Italy in the Age of the Risorgimento, 1790-1870 (Longman, 1983)
Denis Mack Smith, Italy: A Modern History (University of Michigan Press, 1969)
Denis Mack Smith, Victor Emanuel, Cavour and the Risorgimento (Oxford University Press, 1971)
S. Patriarca, The Risorgimento Revisited: Nationalism and Culture in Nineteenth-Century Italy (Springer, 2011)
notes: Dates: start 1820 from 'inspired by the rebellions in the 1820s and 1830s'; end 1871 from 'reached completion in 1871'. The article also says some historians see the Risorgimento continuing to 1918-1920 (irredentism); given in legacy, not in the end year.

Left out: Nice/Niçard exodus and the Niçard Vespers (the article's dates there, Garibaldi elected in 1871, are loosely told); the Pisacane fiasco; Third War battles; culture sections (art, literature, music, films, museums); maps.
Both Bandiera: article says the brothers and their nine companions were executed; I wrote 'with nine companions'.
The Plombières secret arrangements and the Basilicata/Apulia declarations were left out as the article's text is murky.
Garibaldi's 1860 force: 'about a thousand'; the article says swelled to 4,000 within three days; not used.
Cavour's last words are 'purportedly' said, kept hedged. Venetia referendum 'historians suggest' kept hedged.
Article contradictions: Garibaldi was 'elected in 1871 in Nice at the National Assembly' (a French assembly) is odd; left out. Garibald typo in source.
